title: Quick Sort with Complexity
statement:
Sort an array of `n` integers in non-decreasing order.

In the interview you were asked to pick a sorting algorithm, justify its time complexity, and code it while sharing your screen; the candidate chose **quick sort**. Do the same here: implement the sort yourself (quick sort or another `O(n log n)` algorithm) rather than calling a library sort.

The test data includes arrays that are already sorted, sorted in reverse, and filled with many equal values, which are the cases that break a careless quick sort. Your solution must stay `O(n log n)` on all of them.

**Follow-up:** explain why quick sort is `O(n log n)` on average but `O(n^2)` in the worst case, which inputs trigger the worst case for a first-element or last-element pivot, and how a random or median-of-three pivot (or 3-way partitioning) avoids it. Compare it with merge sort in terms of time, extra space and stability. The same interview also asked about Python sets versus tuples and removing null values during data preprocessing; those are discussion topics and not part of this problem.
input_format:
The first line contains an integer `n`.
The second line contains `n` space-separated integers.
output_format: Print the `n` integers in non-decreasing order, separated by single spaces.

examples.explanation: The array in sorted order; the two equal 5s stay adjacent.
A single element is already sorted.
All values are equal, so the output is the same array. A naive partition scheme degrades to O(n^2) here.

hints: Quick sort picks a pivot, partitions the array so smaller values are left and larger values are right, then recurses on both sides.
Always choosing the first or last element as the pivot gives O(n^2) on sorted input. Pick the pivot at random (or take the median of three).
Arrays with many equal values also hurt a two-way partition. Use a 3-way (Dutch national flag) partition, and recurse on the smaller side first (loop on the larger) to keep the recursion depth small.
reference:
import sys

def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split()
    n = int(data[0])
    a = list(map(int, data[1:1 + n]))
    a.sort()
    print(' '.join(map(str, a)))

main()
brute:
import sys

data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n = int(data[0])
a = list(map(int, data[1:1 + n]))
for i in range(1, n):
    x = a[i]
    j = i - 1
    while j >= 0 and a[j] > x:
        a[j + 1] = a[j]
        j -= 1
    a[j + 1] = x
print(' '.join(map(str, a)))
